summary:
Bolivia's 2016 Gender Identity Law grants legal recognition on the basis of self-declared identity through an administrative procedure, permitting a change of name and gender marker without surgery or a medical diagnosis. Gender identity is a protected ground in the country's anti-discrimination legislation.

The 2009 Constitution prohibits discrimination and protects bodily integrity, including a provision against violence under Article 15(II) and a provision on maternity under Article 45(V). The US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report on Bolivia documented that constitutional guarantee alongside persistent societal discrimination against LGBT people.

An April 2024 study in Comparative Politics finds that the 2016 statute was enacted despite low voter support for trans rights. Trans activists secured access to legislators of the ruling party, and heteronormative provisions were adopted in the same period because organised religion and LGBT organisations were both constituencies of the party in government, so contradictory laws stand side by side.

Bolivia's first virtual survey of LGBTI people, published in December 2024, recorded the exclusion of LGBTI people in the country as its central finding. The documented societal exclusion has not been removed by the statutory recognition regime.

Two later developments extend the legal framework: an Inter-American Court of Human Rights opinion issued in January 2018, and civil-registry recognition of free union for same-sex couples in December 2020.

Reporting from August 2014 describes homosexuality as taboo inside the Bolivian armed forces, where gay soldiers recounted discrimination and sanctions in anonymous testimony. An LGBTI collective and human-rights campaigners have demanded openness in the military.
tangentialFactors:
Constitutional protection and lived exposure diverge. The same 2011 reporting that recorded the anti-discrimination guarantee also assessed arbitrary deprivation of life, prison conditions and corruption as national human-rights problems, none of it trans-specific, so a trans visitor who is detained or otherwise enters state custody does so into a system with documented weaknesses.

Reproductive law retains a gendered framing that sits alongside the self-identification statute: the Constitution addresses maternity under Article 45(V) and abortion is governed by Title VIII of the Penal Code. Visitors seeking reproductive or gynaecological care encounter a framework written around maternity rather than gender identity.

The pattern in Bolivia matches a wider regional movement toward administrative recognition: the January 2018 opinion of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights and the December 2020 civil-registry recognition of free union both postdate the 2016 statute, giving a trans visitor regional jurisprudence to cite if a document or registry request is refused.

Bolivia's enactment of a ground-breaking gender identity law against the grain of low public support is presented in the academic literature as a product of insider access to the governing party rather than of shifted public opinion, which means the statute's durability rests partly on party composition. Reversal or obstruction by a differently constituted legislature cannot be ruled out from the sourced material.
localsOnly:
Service in the Bolivian armed forces is affected by a documented culture of secrecy. Reporting of August 2014 records homosexuality as taboo within the military, with gay soldiers describing discrimination and sanctions while speaking anonymously, and an LGBTI collective together with human-rights activists pressing for an open policy. The institutional position of trans personnel is not addressed in that reporting.

Domestic political organising shapes how the recognition regime is maintained. LGBT organisations and organised religion both function as constituencies of the party of government, which is how trans activists obtained access to ruling-party legislators while heteronormative measures advanced in the same legislative period. Advocacy by residents therefore runs through party channels rather than through a settled consensus in the legislature.

Change of name and marker is carried out administratively under the 2016 statute, which places the procedure inside Bolivia's civil-registry system rather than before a court.
outOfScopeNotes:
Practice of the 2016 statute is unresolved in the sourced material. Processing times, fees, the discretion of individual registry offices, regional variation within Bolivia and any documented refusals are not stated in the inventory, so a visitor planning a document-dependent trip cannot verify what a clerk will require in practice.

No sourced item establishes whether gender identity is treated as an aggravating factor or a protected category in criminal sentencing for hate-motivated violence, nor whether such offences have been prosecuted. The inventory contains no dated incidents of violence against trans people in Bolivia with identified perpetrators or outcomes.

The most recent US State Department human-rights reporting in the inventory is from 2011. Whether its assessment of societal discrimination still reflects current conditions is unresolved, and no later State Department assessment is present.

Bolivia's position on trans military service is unresolved. A July 2017 count of 18 countries believed to fully legalise LGBT military service did not single out Bolivia, and the 2014 reporting addresses gay soldiers rather than trans personnel.

The methodology, sample and representativeness of the December 2024 virtual survey are not stated in the inventory beyond its finding of widespread exclusion of LGBTI people, so the scale of that exclusion cannot be quantified from the sourced material.

Abortion under Title VIII of the Penal Code is noted as part of the legal framework but is not assessed here, and access to trans-related healthcare, including hormone therapy and surgical care, is not covered by any item in the inventory.
